questions.q: Name any three supporting characters from the essay and state the specific debate or issue each one is associated with in Sen’s discussion.
questions.a: Correct answer: (1) Krishna and Arjuna – the Bhagavad Gita debate on duty versus consequences; (2) Gargi – the Upanishadic debate with Yajnavalkya on the nature of God; (3) Draupadi – the Mahabharata dialogue urging Yudhishthira to fight rather than renounce. A wrong answer that merely lists names without linking them to the specific argument shows the student treats them as decorative examples rather than functional voices in Sen’s dialectic.

questions.q: Sen writes: “Arjuna’s contrary arguments are not really vanquished… There remains a powerful case for ‘faring well’, and not just ‘faring forward’.” Explain in your own words what Sen means by ‘faring well’ versus ‘faring forward’ and which character represents which position.
questions.a: ‘Faring forward’ is Krishna’s position: do your duty regardless of consequences. ‘Faring well’ is Arjuna’s position: consider the misery and slaughter that duty may cause. A wrong answer that swaps the two or says both mean the same thing reveals the student has not grasped the core philosophical tension Sen highlights.

questions.q: Apply Sen’s method: choose a contemporary Indian public debate (e.g., farm laws, data privacy, uniform civil code) and identify two historical or literary figures from the essay whose perspectives could illuminate opposing sides. Briefly justify your pairing.
questions.a: Example: For the farm laws debate, Krishna’s duty-bound stance (upholding enacted law) could represent the government’s view, while Arjuna’s consequential concern for farmers’ livelihood represents the protesters’ view. A weak answer that picks figures randomly without mapping their philosophical positions to the modern debate shows inability to transfer the analytical framework.

questions.q: Compare the roles of Gargi and Draupadi in Sen’s essay. How does each expand the argumentative tradition beyond male elite discourse? Use textual evidence.
questions.a: Gargi enters a scholarly assembly and challenges the greatest sage Yajnavalkya, proving women’s intellectual participation in ancient philosophical debate. Draupadi, in the Kiratarjuniya, publicly shames Yudhishthira into martial action, showing women’s political voice in epic narrative. An answer that only says “both are women” misses the distinct domains (philosophical vs. political) and the textual specifics Sen provides.

questions.q: Evaluate Sen’s claim that “some of the most powerful arguments in Indian intellectual history have… been about the lives of the least privileged groups.” Does the evidence from the supporting characters (e.g., Kabir, Ravidas, Maitreyi) sufficiently support this claim? Why or why not?
questions.a: Yes, because Kabir (weaver), Ravidas (shoe-maker), and Maitreyi (questioning wealth’s link to immortality) articulate critiques from marginalized positions. However, Sen relies on recorded texts that may filter subaltern voices through elite scribes. An answer that uncritically agrees or dismisses the claim without weighing textual mediation shows lack of evaluative nuance.

questions.q: Create a short dialogue (4-5 exchanges) between two supporting characters from the essay (e.g., Gargi and Kabir) on the topic “Can argumentation alone dismantle caste hierarchy?” Write it in script format.
questions.a: A strong dialogue will have Gargi draw on Upanishadic dialectic (questioning categories) and Kabir draw on Bhakti egalitarianism (rejecting birth-based hierarchy), both acknowledging limits of debate without social action. A weak dialogue that makes them sound identical or ignores their historical contexts shows failure to internalize their distinct argumentative styles.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: In non-fiction essays, supporting characters are the historical, literary, ______, or contemporary figures the author references to illustrate, challenge, or advance the central argument.
Fill in the blank: Imagine ______ an op-ed where the writer quotes Gandhi, Tagore, and a village elder to prove that dissent is Indian.
What is In non-fiction essays, supporting characters? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: In non-fiction essays, supporting characters are the historical, literary, philosophical, or contemporary figures the author references to illustrate, challenge, or advance the central argument.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about In non-fiction essays, supporting characters?
questions.a: Students often treat supporting characters in non-fiction as mere “examples” or “illustrations” of Sen’s points, forgetting that Sen stages them as active participants in a multi-voiced conversation.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify at least three supporting figures in Sen’s essay, explain the specific perspective each represents (e.g., duty vs. consequence, gender voice, caste critique), and articulate how Sen uses their voices to build a pluralistic view of Indian argumentation.
